claim: Retinal waves reliably induce calcium transients in Müller glial cells (MCs).
source: We investigated neuron-glia signaling in the developing retina, where we demonstrate that retinal waves reliably induce calcium transients in Müller glial cells (MCs).
evidence: This is stated as a demonstrated finding in the abstract, supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: During cholinergic waves, MC calcium transients were blocked by muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonists.
source: During cholinergic waves, MC calcium transients were blocked by muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonists, whereas during glutamatergic waves, MC calcium transients were inhibited by ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists, indicating that the responsiveness of MCs changes to match the neurotransmitter used to support retinal waves.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological data in the results section.

claim: During glutamatergic waves, MC calcium transients were inhibited by ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists.
source: During cholinergic waves, MC calcium transients were blocked by muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonists, whereas during glutamatergic waves, MC calcium transients were inhibited by ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists, indicating that the responsiveness of MCs changes to match the neurotransmitter used to support retinal waves.
evidence: This is a direct experimental finding stated in the abstract and supported by pharmacological data in the results section.

claim: The responsiveness of MCs changes to match the neurotransmitter used to support retinal waves.
source: During cholinergic waves, MC calcium transients were blocked by muscarinic acetylcholine receptor antagonists, whereas during glutamatergic waves, MC calcium transients were inhibited by ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists, indicating that the responsiveness of MCs changes to match the neurotransmitter used to support retinal waves.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings showing different receptor involvement at different developmental stages.

claim: The decline in MC calcium transients is caused by a reduction in the amount of glutamate reaching MCs.
source: Using an optical glutamate sensor we show that the decline in MC calcium transients is caused by a reduction in the amount of glutamate reaching MCs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding demonstrated using iGluSnFR optical glutamate sensor experiments.

claim: Neurons and MCs exhibit correlated activity during a critical period of retinal maturation that is enabled by neurotransmitter spillover from retinal synapses.
source: Together, these studies indicate that neurons and MCs exhibit correlated activity during a critical period of retinal maturation that is enabled by neurotransmitter spillover from retinal synapses.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, synthesizing multiple experimental findings.

claim: Glial cells play an important role in developing and maintaining neural circuits.
source: There is rich research history demonstrating the important role glial cells play in developing and maintaining neural circuits (Garrido, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the mature brain, glial cells provide structural scaffolding and create physical barriers that compartmentalize synapses and limit diffusion of neurotransmitters.
source: In the mature brain, glial cells provide structural scaffolding and create physical barriers that compartmentalize synapses and limit diffusion of neurotransmitters.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about glial cell function in the mature brain.

claim: Glial cells express a variety of neurotransmitter receptors.
source: In addition, glial cells express a variety of neurotransmitter receptors.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about glial cells.

claim: Activation of glial receptors causes increases in intracellular calcium that in turn may lead to the secretion of factors that influence circuit function.
source: Activation of glial receptors causes increases in intracellular calcium that in turn may lead to the secretion of factors that influence circuit function (Haydon and Nedergaard, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In the developing brain, glial cells secrete factors that are important for neuronal differentiation, migration, axonal pathfinding and synaptogenesis.
source: In the developing brain, glial cells secrete factors that are important for neuronal differentiation, migration, axonal pathfinding and synaptogenesis (Clarke and Barres, 2013; Garrido, 2013; Chung et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mechanisms that are used for neuron-glial signaling in the developing CNS remain poorly defined.
source: However, the mechanisms that are used for neuron-glial signaling in the developing CNS remain poorly defined.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: There are three types of glial cells in the retina: Müller cells (MCs), astrocytes, and microglial cells.
source: There are three types of glial cells in the retina: Müller cells (MCs), astrocytes, and microglial cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retinal cell types.

claim: MCs are the principal glial cells of the retina.
source: MCs, the principal glial cells of the retina, stretch radially across its thickness from the outer limiting membrane to the inner limiting membrane, sending processes throughout the inner and outer plexiform layers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MCs.

claim: MCs stretch radially across the retina's thickness from the outer limiting membrane to the inner limiting membrane, sending processes throughout the inner and outer plexiform layers.
source: MCs, the principal glial cells of the retina, stretch radially across its thickness from the outer limiting membrane to the inner limiting membrane, sending processes throughout the inner and outer plexiform layers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MC morphology.

claim: MC processes envelop synapses of every neuron type, placing these cells in an ideal position to receive and respond to neuronal signals.
source: MC processes envelop synapses of every neuron type, placing these cells in an ideal position to receive and respond to neuronal signals (Newman and Reichenbach, 1996; Newman, 2004, 2005; Reichenbach and Bringmann, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In adult retina, MCs maintain retinal homeostasis and integrity.
source: In adult retina, MCs maintain retinal homeostasis and integrity (Byrne et al., 2013), and more recently they have been implicated in delivery of retinol to replenish cone opsin chromophore (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MCs have been implicated in delivery of retinol to replenish cone opsin chromophore.
source: In adult retina, MCs maintain retinal homeostasis and integrity (Byrne et al., 2013), and more recently they have been implicated in delivery of retinol to replenish cone opsin chromophore (Xue et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In zebrafish, MC ablation does not affect the laminar organization of the inner plexiform layer.
source: In zebrafish, MC ablation does not affect the laminar organization of the inner plexiform layer (IPL, Randlett et al., 2013) or the structure or organization of synapses in the outer plexiform layer (Williams et al., 2010), in sharp contrast to ablation of MCs in developing (Dubois-Dauphin et al., 2000) and adult mice (Byrne et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2012), which leads to dramatic rearrangements retinal structure (Byrne et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In zebrafish, MC ablation does not affect the structure or organization of synapses in the outer plexiform layer.
source: In zebrafish, MC ablation does not affect the laminar organization of the inner plexiform layer (IPL, Randlett et al., 2013) or the structure or organization of synapses in the outer plexiform layer (Williams et al., 2010), in sharp contrast to ablation of MCs in developing (Dubois-Dauphin et al., 2000) and adult mice (Byrne et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2012), which leads to dramatic rearrangements retinal structure (Byrne et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Ablation of MCs in developing and adult mice leads to dramatic rearrangements of retinal structure.
source: In zebrafish, MC ablation does not affect the laminar organization of the inner plexiform layer (IPL, Randlett et al., 2013) or the structure or organization of synapses in the outer plexiform layer (Williams et al., 2010), in sharp contrast to ablation of MCs in developing (Dubois-Dauphin et al., 2000) and adult mice (Byrne et al., 2013; Shen et al., 2012), which leads to dramatic rearrangements retinal structure (Byrne et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The role of MCs in retinal development has not been fully explored.
source: However, unlike radial glial cells in the cortex and cerebellum, the role of MCs in retinal development has not been fully explored.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: MCs are the last retinal cell types to mature.
source: MCs are the last retinal cell types to mature, integrating into neuronal circuits during the first two postnatal weeks (Jadhav et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2010) when the inner retina is undergoing robust synaptogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: MCs integrate into neuronal circuits during the first two postnatal weeks.
source: MCs are the last retinal cell types to mature, integrating into neuronal circuits during the first two postnatal weeks (Jadhav et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2010) when the inner retina is undergoing robust synaptogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During the first two postnatal weeks, the inner retina is undergoing robust synaptogenesis.
source: MCs are the last retinal cell types to mature, integrating into neuronal circuits during the first two postnatal weeks (Jadhav et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2010) when the inner retina is undergoing robust synaptogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retinal development.

claim: During the developmental period when MCs integrate, the retina is spontaneously active.
source: During this developmental period, the retina is spontaneously active, and ganglion cells (the output cells of the retina) exhibit depolarizations that spread laterally across the retina, a phenomenon termed retinal waves.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retinal development.

claim: Ganglion cells exhibit depolarizations that spread laterally across the retina, a phenomenon termed retinal waves.
source: During this developmental period, the retina is spontaneously active, and ganglion cells (the output cells of the retina) exhibit depolarizations that spread laterally across the retina, a phenomenon termed retinal waves.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retinal waves.

claim: Retinal waves are mediated by circuits that change as the retina matures.
source: These waves are mediated by circuits that change as the retina matures (Blankenship and Feller, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: From postnatal day 1 (P1) to P9, retinal waves are mediated by cholinergic circuits.
source: From postnatal day 1 (P1) to P9, retinal waves are mediated by cholinergic circuits.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retinal wave development.

claim: As bipolar cells integrate into the circuit (P10–P14), the waves become mediated by glutamatergic signaling.
source: As bipolar cells integrate into the circuit (P10–P14), the waves become mediated by glutamatergic signaling.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retinal wave development.

claim: At eye opening (P14), light activated signaling begins and retinal waves cease.
source: At eye opening (P14), light activated signaling begins and retinal waves cease.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about retinal development.

claim: Cholinergic retinal waves are associated with volume release of neurotransmitter.
source: Both cholinergic (Ford et al., 2012) and glutamatergic (Blankenship and Feller, 2010; Firl et al., 2013) retinal waves are associated with volume release of neurotransmitter, where the neurotransmitter is not restricted to the synaptic cleft, but spills out into the extracellular space, allowing activation of receptors on nearby ganglion cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Glutamatergic retinal waves are associated with volume release of neurotransmitter.
source: Both cholinergic (Ford et al., 2012) and glutamatergic (Blankenship and Feller, 2010; Firl et al., 2013) retinal waves are associated with volume release of neurotransmitter, where the neurotransmitter is not restricted to the synaptic cleft, but spills out into the extracellular space, allowing activation of receptors on nearby ganglion cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: During volume release, neurotransmitter is not restricted to the synaptic cleft, but spills out into the extracellular space, allowing activation of receptors on nearby ganglion cells.
source: Both cholinergic (Ford et al., 2012) and glutamatergic (Blankenship and Feller, 2010; Firl et al., 2013) retinal waves are associated with volume release of neurotransmitter, where the neurotransmitter is not restricted to the synaptic cleft, but spills out into the extracellular space, allowing activation of receptors on nearby ganglion cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and describes the mechanism of volume release.

claim: Retinal waves provide a robust source of neurotransmitter that could mediate periodic activation of MCs during retinal development.
source: Hence, these waves provide a robust source of neurotransmitter that could mediate periodic activation of MCs during retinal development.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the known properties of retinal waves.

claim: At P7, a MC displays a simple morphology with its cell body residing in the inner nuclear layer (INL) and a thin, fiber-like process traversing the retina to form part of the inner and outer limiting membranes.
source: At P7 (Figure 1B, bottom), a MC displays a simple morphology with its cell body residing in the inner nuclear layer (INL) and a thin, fiber-like process traversing the retina to form part of the inner and outer limiting membranes (green signal in GLAST::tdTomato, middle panel, and bright punctas in GLASTCreER::GCaMP3, right panel).
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: By P11, MCs have extended many lateral processes into the IPL.
source: By P11 (Figure 1B, middle), MCs have extended many lateral processes (yellow arrows) into the IPL and these continue to grow into the adult form where they closely appose synapses and participate in removing neurotransmitters from the extracellular space (Pow and Crook, 1996).
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MC lateral processes continue to grow into the adult form where they closely appose synapses and participate in removing neurotransmitters from the extracellular space.
source: By P11 (Figure 1B, middle), MCs have extended many lateral processes (yellow arrows) into the IPL and these continue to grow into the adult form where they closely appose synapses and participate in removing neurotransmitters from the extracellular space (Pow and Crook, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: MC calcium transients coincided with RGC compound postsynaptic excitatory currents.
source: Simultaneous two-photon imaging of MCs and whole-cell recordings from RGCs (Figure 1C,D) showed periodic MC calcium transients in the stalks and lateral processes in the IPL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Video 1) that coincided with RGC compound postsynaptic excitatory currents (Blankenship et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from simultaneous imaging and electrophysiology.

claim: The stalks and processes of MCs exhibited similar calcium responses.
source: Since the stalks and processes of MCs exhibited similar calcium responses, we pooled their results together throughout this study.
evidence: This is stated as an observation that justifies pooling data from different MC compartments.

claim: No wave-evoked calcium transients were detected in MC somata.
source: We detected no wave-evoked calcium transients in other parts of MCs outside the IPL (i.e., in their somata, data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as a negative finding from the experiments.

claim: The percentage of ROIs that responded to a wave was 42 ± 10.2% at P7.
source: The percentage of regions of interest (ROIs, which correspond to compartments of individual MCs, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1) that responded to a wave (termed responsive MCs) was high at P7 (42 ± 10.2%, 1326 ROIs from 11 retinas) and at P9 (48 ± 4.6%, 3027 ROIs from 14 retinas), but significantly lower at P11 (13 ± 2.2%, 872 ROIs from 6 retinas, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the imaging experiments.

claim: The percentage of ROIs that responded to a wave was 48 ± 4.6% at P9.
source: The percentage of regions of interest (ROIs, which correspond to compartments of individual MCs, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1) that responded to a wave (termed responsive MCs) was high at P7 (42 ± 10.2%, 1326 ROIs from 11 retinas) and at P9 (48 ± 4.6%, 3027 ROIs from 14 retinas), but significantly lower at P11 (13 ± 2.2%, 872 ROIs from 6 retinas, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the imaging experiments.

claim: The percentage of ROIs that responded to a wave was significantly lower at P11 (13 ± 2.2%).
source: The percentage of regions of interest (ROIs, which correspond to compartments of individual MCs, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1) that responded to a wave (termed responsive MCs) was high at P7 (42 ± 10.2%, 1326 ROIs from 11 retinas) and at P9 (48 ± 4.6%, 3027 ROIs from 14 retinas), but significantly lower at P11 (13 ± 2.2%, 872 ROIs from 6 retinas, Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the imaging experiments.

claim: MCs express a variety of neurotransmitter receptors, including glutamatergic and cholinergic receptors.
source: As MCs express a variety of neurotransmitter receptors, including glutamatergic and cholinergic receptors (Wakakura and Yamamoto, 1994; Belmonte et al., 2000), MC calcium transients at different ages could be evoked by different neurotransmitters released during retinal waves.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Control application of extracellular solution (ACSF) did not evoke a MC response, indicating that the pressure injection itself did not evoke calcium transients through mechanical stimulation.
source: Control application of extracellular solution (artificial cerebrospinal fluid [ACSF]) did not evoke a MC response, indicating that the pressure injection itself did not evoke calcium transients through mechanical stimulation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating that the observed responses are not due to mechanical stimulation.

claim: When ATP (1 mM) was applied, robust calcium transients were induced that were inhibited by the P2 receptor blocker suramin (100 μM).
source: When adenosine tri-phosphate (ATP, 1 mM) was applied, robust calcium transients were induced that were inhibited by the P2 receptor blocker suramin (100 μM; Figure 2D), as seen previously in the adult retina (Uckermann et al., 2002; Newman, 2004; Metea and Newman, 2006).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from focal application experiments.

claim: MCs responded to acetylcholine (ACh, 1 mM).
source: MCs also responded to acetylcholine (ACh, 1 mM; Figure 2B,C; Video 2), as described in cortical astrocytes (Takata et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from focal application experiments.

claim: ACh-evoked MC calcium transients were reduced by the muscarinic ACh receptor antagonist atropine (50 µM).
source: These ACh-evoked MC calcium transients were reduced by the muscarinic ACh receptor antagonist atropine (50 µM; Figure 2E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Similar ACh- and ATP-evoked MC calcium transients were also observed at P9 and at P11.
source: Similar ACh- and ATP-evoked MC calcium transients were also observed at P9 (during the transition from cholinergic to glutamatergic waves) and at P11 (during glutamatergic waves), indicating that MCs express multiple neurotransmitter receptors prior to eye opening (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is an experimental finding showing that MC responses to agonists persist across developmental stages.

claim: MCs express multiple neurotransmitter receptors prior to eye opening.
source: Similar ACh- and ATP-evoked MC calcium transients were also observed at P9 (during the transition from cholinergic to glutamatergic waves) and at P11 (during glutamatergic waves), indicating that MCs express multiple neurotransmitter receptors prior to eye opening (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings showing responses to multiple agonists.

claim: Wave-induced MC calcium transients at P7 were blocked by the muscarinic ACh receptor (mAChR) antagonist atropine (50 µM).
source: Interestingly, this ACh is released by cholinergic amacrine cells that also release ATP (Duarte et al., 1999). Thus, we tested the effect of AChR and ATP receptor blockers on wave-induced MC calcium transients. Although the wave-induced transients were blocked by the muscarinic ACh receptor (mAChR) antagonist atropine (50 µM; Figure 2G), they were not blocked by the ATP receptor antagonist suramin (100 μM; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from pharmacological experiments during retinal waves.

claim: Wave-induced MC calcium transients at P7 were not blocked by the ATP receptor antagonist suramin (100 μM).
source: Interestingly, this ACh is released by cholinergic amacrine cells that also release ATP (Duarte et al., 1999). Thus, we tested the effect of AChR and ATP receptor blockers on wave-induced MC calcium transients. Although the wave-induced transients were blocked by the muscarinic ACh receptor (mAChR) antagonist atropine (50 µM; Figure 2G), they were not blocked by the ATP receptor antagonist suramin (100 μM; Figure 2H).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from pharmacological experiments during retinal waves.

claim: At P7, MC calcium transients are evoked by volume release of ACh, but not by ATP, and these transients are mediated by mAChRs on MCs.
source: Therefore, we conclude that at P7, MC calcium transients are evoked by volume release of ACh, but not by ATP, and these transients are mediated by mAChRs on MCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological experiments.

claim: At P9, circuits mediating retinal waves change from cholinergic to glutamatergic.
source: At P9, circuits mediating retinal waves change from cholinergic to glutamatergic (Blankenship and Feller, 2010), and glutamatergic synapses between bipolar cells and their postsynaptic targets first appear (Hoon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Glutamatergic synapses between bipolar cells and their postsynaptic targets first appear at P9.
source: At P9, circuits mediating retinal waves change from cholinergic to glutamatergic (Blankenship and Feller, 2010), and glutamatergic synapses between bipolar cells and their postsynaptic targets first appear (Hoon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Short applications of ACh induced calcium transients that were blocked by the mAChR blocker atropine at P9.
source: To determine the involvement of cholinergic transmission in MC signaling at this stage of development, we examined their response to focal application of ACh. Short applications of ACh induced calcium transients that were blocked by the mAChR blocker atropine at P9 (Figure 2E), but bath application of atropine did not change the percentage of wave-induced MC calcium transients (57 ± 12.6% in control and 60.2 ± 7.8% in atropine; p = 0.54, n = 4).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from focal application experiments at P9.

claim: Bath application of atropine did not change the percentage of wave-induced MC calcium transients at P9 (57 ± 12.6% in control and 60.2 ± 7.8% in atropine; p = 0.54, n = 4).
source: Short applications of ACh induced calcium transients that were blocked by the mAChR blocker atropine at P9 (Figure 2E), but bath application of atropine did not change the percentage of wave-induced MC calcium transients (57 ± 12.6% in control and 60.2 ± 7.8% in atropine; p = 0.54, n = 4).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from pharmacological experiments during waves at P9.

claim: Cholinergic signaling does not mediate neuron-MC signaling at P9.
source: These results indicate that cholinergic signaling does not mediate neuron-MC signaling at this age.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the atropine experiments at P9.

claim: Application of exogenous L-glutamate reliably evoked MC calcium transients.
source: We then determined the role of glutamate in triggering these responses. Application of exogenous L-glutamate reliably evoked MC calcium transients (Figure 3A–C; Video 3).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from focal application experiments.

claim: L-glutamate-evoked MC calcium transients were not blocked by atropine, ruling out the possibility that this agonist acted indirectly by stimulating release of ACh from amacrine cells.
source: These responses were not blocked by atropine, ruling out the possibility that this agonist acted indirectly by stimulating release of ACh from amacrine cells.
evidence: This is a control experiment ruling out indirect effects of glutamate application.

claim: L-glutamate-evoked MC calcium transients were significantly reduced by a cocktail of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists (iGluR: 20 μM DNQX, 50 μM D-AP5).
source: L-glutamate-evoked MC calcium transients were significantly reduced by a cocktail of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists (iGluR: 20 μM AMPA/kainate receptor antagonist DNQX, 50 μM NMDA receptor antagonist D-AP5; Figure 3D), but were only slightly reduced by a mixture of metabotropic glutamate receptor antagonists (mGluR: 8 μM LY341495, 100 μM MCPG, 100 μM MTEP; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from pharmacological experiments.

claim: L-glutamate-evoked MC calcium transients were only slightly reduced by a mixture of metabotropic glutamate receptor antagonists (mGluR: 8 μM LY341495, 100 μM MCPG, 100 μM MTEP).
source: L-glutamate-evoked MC calcium transients were significantly reduced by a cocktail of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists (iGluR: 20 μM AMPA/kainate receptor antagonist DNQX, 50 μM NMDA receptor antagonist D-AP5; Figure 3D), but were only slightly reduced by a mixture of metabotropic glutamate receptor antagonists (mGluR: 8 μM LY341495, 100 μM MCPG, 100 μM MTEP; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is an experimental finding from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Blocking AMPA receptors produced substantial but incomplete inhibition of the L-glutamate-evoked response.
source: Blocking AMPA receptors produced substantial but incomplete inhibition of the L-glutamate-evoked response, whereas blocking NMDA receptors had no significant effect.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Blocking NMDA receptors had no significant effect on L-glutamate-evoked MC calcium transients.
source: Blocking AMPA receptors produced substantial but incomplete inhibition of the L-glutamate-evoked response, whereas blocking NMDA receptors had no significant effect.
evidence: This is an experimental finding from pharmacological experiments.

claim: Glutamate elicits MC calcium transients primarily through activation of AMPA receptors, although a modest contribution of mGluRs is also observed.
source: These results suggest that glutamate elicits MC calcium transients primarily through activation of AMPA receptors, although a modest contribution of mGluRs is also observed.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the pharmacological experiments with glutamate receptor antagonists.

claim: The reduction of L-glutamate-evoked calcium transients by glutamate receptor blockers occurred at all ages (P7, P9, P11), not just during the period when glutamatergic waves predominate.
source: Notably, the reduction of L-glutamate-evoked calcium transients by glutamate receptor blockers occurred at all ages, not just during the period when glutamatergic waves predominate, indicating that MCs express glutamate receptors throughout this period of development.
evidence: This is an observation from experiments conducted at multiple developmental ages.

claim: MCs express glutamate receptors throughout the period from P7 to P11.
source: Notably, the reduction of L-glutamate-evoked calcium transients by glutamate receptor blockers occurred at all ages, not just during the period when glutamatergic waves predominate, indicating that MCs express glutamate receptors throughout this period of development.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that glutamate receptor blockers are effective at all ages tested.

claim: At P11, wave-induced MC calcium transients were dramatically reduced.
source: However, at P11, wave-induced MC calcium transients were dramatically reduced (Figures 1E, 3G,H) although robust glutamate spillover occurs at this age (Blankenship et al., 2009; Firl et al., 2013) and exogenous glutamate induced MC calcium transients (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from imaging during retinal waves at P11.

claim: Robust glutamate spillover occurs at P11.
source: However, at P11, wave-induced MC calcium transients were dramatically reduced (Figures 1E, 3G,H) although robust glutamate spillover occurs at this age (Blankenship et al., 2009; Firl et al., 2013) and exogenous glutamate induced MC calcium transients (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The reduction of MC activity at P11 is a consequence of the upregulation of glutamate transporters.
source: We hypothesize that this reduction of MC activity is a consequence of the upregulation of glutamate transporters at P11 (Pow and Barnett, 2000; Pannicke et al., 2002), which may limit the amount of glutamate that reaches MC membranes to induce calcium transients.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous literature showing upregulation of glutamate transporters.

claim: Glutamate transporters are upregulated at P11.
source: We hypothesize that this reduction of MC activity is a consequence of the upregulation of glutamate transporters at P11 (Pow and Barnett, 2000; Pannicke et al., 2002), which may limit the amount of glutamate that reaches MC membranes to induce calcium transients.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At P11, DL-TBOA drastically increased the percentage of responsive MCs from 13 ± 2.2% to 61 ± 4.3%.
source: At P11, DL-TBOA drastically increased the percentage of responsive MCs from 13 ± 2.2% to 61 ± 4.3% (Figure 3G,H; 872 ROIs in control and 1342 ROIs in DL-TBOA from 6 retinas).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments with the glutamate transporter blocker.

claim: At P9, DL-TBOA did not significantly change the percentage of responsive MCs, increasing only slightly from 48 ± 4.5% to 58 ± 10.0%.
source: Interestingly, at P9, DL-TBOA did not significantly change the percentage of responsive MCs, increasing only slightly from 48 ± 4.5% to 58 ± 10.0% (Figure 3E,F; 3027 ROIs in control and 3549 ROIs in DL-TBOA from 8 retinas).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from experiments with the glutamate transporter blocker.

claim: At ages earlier than P11, transporters do not strongly regulate glutamate spillover.
source: We conclude that at ages earlier than P11, transporters do not strongly regulate glutamate spillover, but by P11, they mediate significant glutamate uptake, decreasing the amount of glutamate that reaches MC receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DL-TBOA experiments at different ages.

claim: By P11, glutamate transporters mediate significant glutamate uptake, decreasing the amount of glutamate that reaches MC receptors.
source: We conclude that at ages earlier than P11, transporters do not strongly regulate glutamate spillover, but by P11, they mediate significant glutamate uptake, decreasing the amount of glutamate that reaches MC receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DL-TBOA experiments showing a large effect at P11.

claim: The iGluSnFR signal is proportional to the amount of glutamate reaching the membrane.
source: The iGluSnFR signal is proportional to the amount of glutamate reaching the membrane (Marvin et al., 2013); thus, the lack of fluorescence in the INL where MC cell bodies are located indicates that during early development there is little glutamate release outside of the IPL.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the original iGluSnFR paper.

claim: During early development there is little glutamate release outside of the IPL.
source: The iGluSnFR signal is proportional to the amount of glutamate reaching the membrane (Marvin et al., 2013); thus, the lack of fluorescence in the INL where MC cell bodies are located indicates that during early development there is little glutamate release outside of the IPL.
evidence: This is an inference from the lack of iGluSnFR signal in the INL.

claim: At both P9 and P11, the processes of neurons that expressed iGluSnFR exhibited large glutamate transients that propagated throughout the field of view with each retinal wave.
source: At both P9 and P11, the processes of neurons that expressed iGluSnFR exhibited large glutamate transients that propagated throughout the field of view with each retinal wave (Figure 4A,C; 160 ROIs from 5 retinas at P9 and 160 ROIs from 5 retinas at P11; Video 4), consistent with the key role played by glutamate in inducing retinal waves at these ages.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from iGluSnFR imaging in neurons.

claim: Many MCs expressing iGluSnFR displayed glutamate transients during P9 waves (38 ± 4%, 1023 ROIs from 5 retinas).
source: In contrast, although many MCs expressing iGluSnFR displayed glutamate transients during P9 waves (38 ± 4%, 1023 ROIs from 5 retinas, Figure 4B,C), the percentage of responsive MCs decreased dramatically by P11 (6 ± 2%, 269 ROIs from 5 retinas at P11; Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from iGluSnFR imaging in MCs.

claim: The percentage of responsive MCs expressing iGluSnFR decreased dramatically by P11 (6 ± 2%, 269 ROIs from 5 retinas).

source: BGs express calcium permeable AMPARs that are activated by glutamate released at parallel and climbing fiber synapses (Bergles et al., 1997; Clark and Barbour, 1997; Piet and Jahr, 2007), raising the possibility that AMPAR expression may be a conserved properties of radial-type astroglial cells.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In vivo studies indicate that calcium signaling in BGs during locomotion depends on the activation of AMPARs.
source: Although the role of AMPARs in BG activity is still controversial (Müller et al., 1996; Iino et al., 2001; Nimmerjahn et al., 2009), in vivo studies indicate that calcium signaling in BGs during locomotion depends on the activation of AMPARs (Nimmerjahn et al., 2009) and disruption of this signaling (Iino et al., 2001; Saab et al., 2012), results in prolonged synaptic events that are associated with altered motor behavior and motor learning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Disruption of AMPAR signaling in BGs results in prolonged synaptic events that are associated with altered motor behavior and motor learning.

claim: The findings in the developing retina differ from studies performed in the adult retina, in which glutamate does not evoke calcium transients in MCs.
